runs.analysis: Candidate A is far more specific and decision-useful. It gives concrete parameters, quantified risks, detailed scenarios, and many fallbacks with trade-offs, and it ties each document to prior-stage facts. Its flaws: several scenario fields are stringified JSON in inconsistent formats, some items are phrased as questions, some figures are invented, and the geotechnical timeline is internally inconsistent (testing scheduled after the June 2027 hard stop). Candidate B is complete (12 documents) and cleanly formatted, but it is shallow. Its essential_information mostly restates the steps_to_create, its risks and scenarios are generic, its fallbacks are boilerplate, and it has a stray dollar-sign slip. A offers much more value to downstream stages despite its format and consistency issues.

Candidate A covers all 12 documents and follows the schema: scenarios are plain strings and the lists are consistent. It is plan-specific, using the 14 km span, 100 m depth, €4-6B contingency, 5/10/15% triggers, June 2027 gate and Azores-Gibraltar fault. Its flaws are minor: the Phasing document says "4-5 year phases" next to phases of ~6-7, ~5-6 and ~4-5 years, the Energy document mixes "$" with "€", and some fallbacks are generic. Candidate B is deeper in places, for example EU state aid and TEN-T, tranche-verification mechanics, and detailed geotechnical protocols. But several worst_case and best_case fields are stringified JSON objects or lists, which is inconsistent and violates the string schema. Some essential_information items are lists of questions rather than content specs. It invents precise fabricated specifics and has factual slips ("ESA's Gannt Project", "Cross-Lot Tunnel"). It is extremely verbose and appears truncated mid-document, with the last three documents missing from what was shown. A is more complete, consistent and format-faithful; B's extra depth does not offset these defects.

Both candidates cover the same six documents with the same metadata and the same schema fields. Both tie their content to the upstream decisions: Pragmatic Scale-Up, the 60% tenant threshold, the 36-month RTE buffer, the 128.8 km² buffer holding costs, and Substation 1 isolation.

Candidate A is tight and mostly consistent. Its essential_information items are specific, and some are good analytical asks, such as the NPV/IRR comparison of a 36-month versus a 48-month RTE timeline and the lead time between the tenant trigger and the collateral date. Weaknesses:
- The risks are mostly qualitative.
- It never addresses FX or USD exposure, which the plan prompt requires.
- It has little quantification of consequences.
- Each document gets only three fallbacks.
- The scenarios are thinner.
- There is a stray "4 GW target" and an unsupported "€1B+" feasibility figure.
- Some essential-information items just restate the description.

Candidate B is far more detailed and decision-useful for the downstream stage that writes the documents.
- Its essential_information is structured into concrete, checkable content: the budget breakdown, the funding gates, the success criteria, the holding-cost arithmetic (€50–75k/ha for 18 months, about €1.3B, which is plausible), the 38.6 km² offset versus 89.2 km² reserve split, and the cross-dependency matrix.
- It includes FX hedging and the USD/EUR split.
- It quantifies risks and consequences.
- It offers many fallbacks that are actually different approaches.

Weaknesses:
- It is very verbose.
- It invents a lot of numbers, such as the €12.5–37.5M skills academy figure.
- Its best-case scenarios are rosy, for example "binding RTE Phase 2 allocation before Phase 1 financing", which sits uneasily with the "No Grid Pre-Commitment" decision.
- It cites a "Q4 2026 DGSI workshop per project-plan.md" and some example precedents that may be invented.
- It has a few internal tensions.

Overall, B's specificity, quantification, FX coverage and richer scenarios and fallbacks outweigh its verbosity and some invented figures. A's brevity leaves it too generic to guide the next stage.

Candidate A is much richer and more decision-useful for downstream stages. Its essential-information items are concrete: the 32.2 / 128.8 / 38.6 / 89.2 km² land split, the €50k–75k/ha holding-cost arithmetic (about €1.3B over 18 months), collateral by upgrade category, trigger points, and isolation sub-items. Its risks are specific and quantified and tie back to the plan's decisions. Its scenarios are detailed, and it offers many practical fallbacks. Its weaknesses are some speculative or invented figures (NPV, bps, BESS costs), a grid best case that implies a binding Phase 2 RTE allocation before Phase 1 financing (awkward against 'No Grid Pre-Commitment'), and verbosity. Candidate B is faithful but thin. It has 4–5 essential items per document, generic risks, one-sentence scenarios with little quantification, and only three fallbacks, some of them questionable (sovereign-first pivot contradicting the deferred-sovereign decision, 'open-source hardware stacks' for AI compute). A better fulfils the purpose of a content spec.

Candidate A is much deeper and more decision-useful. Each document has 8–12 essential-information items, many risks, and several fallbacks. The content is concrete and plan-specific: strike thresholds and cumulative logic, fee-formula, trigger and collateral items, first/last-segment edge cases, cost-category exclusions, and a PRM compliance matrix. It ties these to the plan's constraints (€900M capacity budget, €200M float, €300M reserve, T+3 and T+5 timings, Months 6/18/30). Its flaws are minor: placeholders in the charter ("Month X", "€XXM"), some speculative invented figures, BEUC mislabeled as a disability body, small version/month inconsistencies, and embedded-JSON strings in the enforcement document's scenario fields. Candidate B is faithful to the strategic-decision framing but thin: 4–6 essential items per document, only 3 fallbacks, brief risks and scenarios. Its charter reads like a decision summary and omits budget, scope, governance and metrics. Several fallbacks are weak or conflict with the "realistic, not aggressive" instruction (revert to Pioneer, parallel aggressive timeline). A is more useful downstream and offers more insight.

A is concise and consistent but thin. Its Charter essential information is mostly meta-process about levers and scenarios, and some fallbacks are weak or self-contradictory. B is far more specific and decision-useful: it gives budget lines, metric definitions, strike accumulation and appeal logic, pool governance, and cost-category exclusions, with many concrete risks and actionable fallbacks. B has flaws: placeholders such as "Month X" and "€XXM", a few factual slips (BEUC called a disability body, XML schema), speculative invented figures, and JSON-in-string formatting for one document's scenarios. Overall B's depth outweighs these.

Both candidates cover the same seven documents with the same schema. B is more detailed and decision-useful, but it has temporal and numerical errors. A is thinner and has one clear content mismatch.

Candidate A: It is concise and mostly consistent with the stated gates, thresholds and roles. Its Project Charter essential_information is wrong for a charter. It describes a strategic-decisions summary (levers, choices, synergies and conflicts, Lever IDs) and omits authorization, scope, budget, gates and decision rights. The other documents have only 4-5 fairly generic essential items each. Some fallbacks lean on apps, which sits uneasily with the plan's no-apps constraint.

Candidate B: The charter content is right for a charter: authority, SMART goal, gates, budget split with the €300k MCR, constraints, critical path, risks and metrics. Other documents have 9-12 specific essential items and 8-10 risks, such as MCR trigger conditions and tiered release, an alert-level action matrix with time-to-activation targets, audit sampling rates, MOU term and resource commitments, and installation SLAs with unit-cost assumptions. Fallbacks are numerous, concrete and often costed. Flaws: it uses dates that contradict the May 2026 start (charter by Jan 31, 2026; contracts mid-March; Month 4 as April 30). It has internal numeric nonsense (€2.3M of the initial €2.0M). It invents outcomes (35-50 deaths prevented, 8,500 residents). It confuses the Month 2 and Month 4 gates in places. It has stray formatting characters in the MOU worst and best cases. Its scenarios are very long.

Verdict: B's errors are mostly in the scenario narratives and some dates. A's charter spec is fundamentally mismatched and A is shallow elsewhere. B better gives downstream stages specific content, risks and scenarios, so B is somewhat better.

A is far more detailed and plan-specific: 8–12 essential items per document, quantified risks and scenarios, and concrete fallbacks, all tied to Leipzig, the gates, the MCR, GDPR, and installation targets. Its flaws are real. Some dates conflict with today's date (a January 2026 charter, mid-March contracts, Month 4 on April 30). The MCR worst case has "€2.3M of the initial €2.0M". Several numbers are invented, and one best-case string is malformed. B is cleaner but thin and generic, with 4–6 items per document and few quantities. Its charter spec describes the strategic-decisions document rather than a project charter, which is a clear mismatch. A is more useful for downstream stages despite its inconsistencies.
